candidates.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Bench Press

distinctFrom.why: pressing one dumbbell at a time adds an anti-rotation core demand the two-arm version does not have

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Same flat-bench mechanics as the bilateral version otherwise.

candidates.name: Alternating Dumbbell Bench Press

distinctFrom.why: alternating one arm at a time changes the anti-rotation demand and time-under-tension pattern versus pressing both together

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Vocabulary gap: the app's real deriveLaterality() (src/lib/exerciseMetadata.js) has only bilateral/unilateral values keyed off name regex; 'alternating' names are not matched and would derive to bilateral at seed time. This candidate's schema-level laterality is 'alternating' per EL-2, but ships with a known mismatch against the app's internal derivation until that regex is extended - flagged for the lead.

candidates.name: Floor Fly (Dumbbell)

distinctFrom.why: lying on the floor rather than a bench shortens the bottom range of motion, the same range/depth relationship as Floor Press (Dumbbell) to Dumbbell Bench Press

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: No bench required, common home-gym substitution for the standard fly.

candidates.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Fly

distinctFrom.why: one arm at a time adds an anti-rotation core demand and lets the working side get a longer stretch, unlike the bilateral version

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Same flat-bench mechanics otherwise.

candidates.name: Seated Single-Arm Dumbbell Press

distinctFrom.why: seated removes leg drive and lower-back involvement, the same standing/seated split the corpus already uses for Dumbbell Shoulder Press vs Seated Dumbbell Press

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: axialLoad came back null; overridden to true to match the existing curated value for Seated Dumbbell Press (a seated overhead press still loads the spine axially).

candidates.name: Z-Press (Dumbbell)

distinctFrom.why: seated on the floor with legs straight out and no back support, removing every stabiliser but the trunk itself - a support condition change, not merely a seated/standing swap

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Demand axes came back null; overridden to exactly match the existing Barbell Z-Press's curated values (seated on the floor, floor access required, axially loaded, stable-not-supported balance) since the body position is identical, only the implement differs.

candidates.name: Incline Lateral Raise (Bench)

distinctFrom.why: lying prone on an incline bench removes any torso swing/momentum the standing version allows, changing the balance and support condition, not just the plane

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Distinct from the standing 'Leaning Lateral Raise' and 'Seated Lateral Raise' rows, which both keep the torso upright.

candidates.name: Alternating Dumbbell Front Raise

distinctFrom.why: alternating arms changes the anti-rotation/core demand and rest-per-side pattern versus raising both together

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Same alternating-laterality vocabulary gap noted on Alternating Dumbbell Bench Press applies here.

candidates.name: Seated Bent-Over Rear Delt Raise

distinctFrom.why: seated with the torso bent forward over the knees, distinct from the existing row's prone/incline-bench-supported position and from standing bent-over variants

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: One of the most common gym rear-delt exercises; fills a real gap between the prone incline and side-lying variants already in the corpus.

candidates.name: Dumbbell Upright Row

distinctFrom.why: implement differs (a dumbbell in each hand travels its own path rather than a fixed bar), changing the wrist and grip demand

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: never_auto to match the mechanical caution already implied by the brief for the barbell version.

candidates.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row (Bench-Supported)

distinctFrom.why: the existing 'Dumbbell Row' row is tagged bilateral (both dumbbells worked together); this is the classic one-arm-at-a-time bench-kneeling row, a distinct laterality

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: One of the most standard gym exercises and a genuine gap: the existing 'Dumbbell Row' entry is bilateral, so no unilateral bench-supported row exists in the corpus today. axialLoad came back null; overridden to false since one hand and knee are braced on the bench, removing standing spinal loading (matching Chest-Supported Row (Barbell)'s false value).

candidates.name: Seal Row (Dumbbell)

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (two dumbbells vs a barbell), letting each arm move independently through a slightly different path

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Requires a raised bench platform, same setup logic as the barbell version.

candidates.name: Incline Dumbbell Pullover

distinctFrom.why: an inclined bench changes the shoulder angle and shortens the top-range stretch compared with the flat-bench version

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: subregion left null to match the existing Dumbbell Pullover's own null subregion (pullover isn't tracked on the chest angle taxonomy in this corpus).

candidates.name: Spider Curl (Dumbbell)

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (two independently-moving dumbbells vs a fixed barbell), the same distinction the corpus already draws for other curl variants (Barbell Curl vs Dumbbell Curl)

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Long-head-biased prone-incline curl position, same as the barbell version.

candidates.name: Dumbbell Drag Curl

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs; dumbbells also let the drag path continue further back at the torso than a barbell can clear

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Long-head-biased, matching the barbell drag curl's subregion.

candidates.name: Dumbbell Reverse Curl

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (dumbbell vs barbell), the same distinction already drawn between the corpus's other curl families

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Overhand/pronated grip, brachialis-biased, matching the barbell reverse curl.

candidates.name: Single-Arm Overhead Dumbbell Tricep Extension

distinctFrom.why: one dumbbell in one hand rather than one dumbbell held with both hands changes the laterality and adds an anti-lateral-flexion core demand

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Very standard gym accessory movement.

candidates.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Skull Crusher

distinctFrom.why: one dumbbell per arm moving independently rather than two dumbbells moving together, adding a per-side stability demand

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: overheadPosition came back null; overridden to true to match Dumbbell Skull Crusher's curated value (same overhead-arm-extension phase).

candidates.name: Dumbbell Glute Bridge

distinctFrom.why: implement differs (loaded dumbbell across the hips vs bodyweight-only), same movement pattern as the existing bodyweight row

sources: Bret Contreras, Glute Lab
candidates.notes: Natural loaded progression from the bodyweight Glute Bridge before a barbell hip thrust.

candidates.name: Cossack Squat (Dumbbell)

distinctFrom.why: goes to full squat depth on one side with the other leg extended straight, versus the lateral lunge's partial-depth stepping pattern - a range/depth class difference

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: subregion left null: adductors has no subregion taxonomy in the current corpus (empty list), so none is invented per the method's rule.

candidates.name: Deficit Dumbbell Calf Raise (Standing)

distinctFrom.why: standing on a raised platform (plate or step) extends the bottom range of motion for a deeper stretch, a range/depth class difference

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Same gastrocnemius bias as the standard standing raise, deeper range only.

candidates.name: Lying Dumbbell Leg Curl

distinctFrom.why: new movement family for this corpus: hamstring knee-flexion isolation performed lying prone holding a single dumbbell between the feet, in place of a leg-curl machine

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Old-school home-gym substitute for a lying leg curl machine; distinctFrom points to no directly analogous existing row since no dumbbell-family leg curl exists yet.

candidates.name: Weighted Dumbbell Crunch

distinctFrom.why: a crunch is a short-range spinal-flexion movement (shoulders lift off the floor) rather than a full sit-up to seated, matching the existing bodyweight Crunch vs Weighted Sit-Up split

sources: Brad Schoenfeld, Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
candidates.notes: Holds a single dumbbell on the chest or overhead for added resistance on the standard crunch.

candidates.name: Dumbbell Dead Bug

distinctFrom.why: implement differs (dumbbells held overhead in each hand add an anti-extension load vs bodyweight-only), same base movement pattern

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Anti-extension core work; loaded progression from the bodyweight version.

candidates.name: Dumbbell Woodchop

distinctFrom.why: a diagonal rotational chop pattern through the hips and trunk rather than a lateral flexion hold at the hip

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Rotation-subregion core movement, standing, matching the Russian Twist/rotation family already in the corpus.

candidates.name: Seated Dumbbell Shrug

distinctFrom.why: seated removes any leg/hip drive assistance the standing version allows, isolating the traps more strictly

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: subregion left null to match the corpus's convention that no trap exercise carries a subregion value.

candidates.name: Dumbbell Reverse Wrist Curl

distinctFrom.why: implement family differs (dumbbell vs barbell), matching the corpus's existing Dumbbell Wrist Curl vs Barbell Wrist Curl split

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Extensor-focused counterpart to Dumbbell Wrist Curl.

rejected.name: Neutral-Grip Dumbbell Bench Press
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 — a standard dumbbell bench press grip is already neutral by default hand position; no alternate-grip variant exists to distinguish it from

rejected.name: Reverse-Grip Dumbbell Fly
rejected.reason: unattested — a fly's palms face a fixed direction throughout the arc; there is no meaningful grip variant to name separately

rejected.name: Incline Bench Dumbbell Row
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Chest-Supported Row (Dumbbell)' — the same mechanics under a different name

rejected.name: Pendlay-Style Dumbbell Row
rejected.reason: unattested — Pendlay row is a barbell-specific dead-stop-from-floor technique, not documented as a dumbbell exercise in mainstream coaching literature

rejected.name: Dumbbell Sumo Squat
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Sumo Squat (Glute Focus)' — same movement already in the corpus tagged by training focus; a quads-primary re-tag is not a new training stimulus

rejected.name: JM Press (Dumbbell)
rejected.reason: unattested — JM press is a barbell-specific hybrid between a skull crusher and a close-grip press; no standard dumbbell adaptation is documented

rejected.name: Close-Grip Dumbbell Press
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Dumbbell Squeeze Press' — pressing two dumbbells together with a close grip is the same movement already in the corpus

rejected.name: Suitcase Crunch
rejected.reason: unattested — sources disagree whether this names a lying oblique crunch or a standing anti-lateral-flexion hold; not a single well-defined canonical movement

rejected.name: Copenhagen Plank (Dumbbell)
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 — the brief directs that sumo squat variants already cover the adductor training need for this family

rejected.name: Dumbbell Neck Lateral Flexion
rejected.reason: unattested — this corpus's convention loads neck work with a plate or harness, not a hand-held dumbbell; no attested dumbbell-in-hand neck movement was found

rejected.name: Dumbbell Suitcase Deadlift
rejected.reason: owned by carries inventory — unilateral suitcase-position pull-to-carry setup belongs with the loaded-carry family
